reference.source: Apley & Solomon / standard sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: Presents with diffuse or peri-patellar anterior knee pain aggravated by loaded knee flexion such as squatting, stairs, kneeling, and prolonged sitting (the theatre sign)
It is a diagnosis based on the pattern of anterior knee pain after excluding other structural causes, and imaging is usually normal
It is most common in adolescents and young adults, particularly active females
Contributing factors include quadriceps and gluteal weakness, dynamic knee valgus, hip control deficits, and training overload rather than a single structural lesion
The old label chondromalacia patellae describes cartilage softening but correlates poorly with symptoms and is not synonymous with the syndrome
Examination may reveal pain on patellar compression, poor lower-limb alignment on a single-leg squat, and quadriceps or hip abductor weakness
First-line management is exercise therapy targeting the quadriceps and hip musculature, combined with load management and activity modification
Adjuncts include patellar taping, appropriate footwear or orthoses, and attention to biomechanics and training errors
Distinguish it from patellar instability, patellar tendinopathy, and referred pain, which need different treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Patellofemoral pain arises from excessive or maldistributed stress across the patellofemoral joint. Imbalance in the forces controlling patellar tracking, weakness of the quadriceps and hip abductors, dynamic valgus, and altered lower-limb alignment concentrate load on the retropatellar and peripatellar tissues. Repetitive overload of richly innervated subchondral bone and soft tissue, rather than cartilage damage alone, generates pain.
additionalDifferentials: Chondral or osteochondral lesions and early osteoarthritis
Osgood-Schlatter or Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease in adolescents
Referred pain from the hip (including slipped capital femoral epiphysis in adolescents) or lumbar spine
additionalInvestigations: Primarily a clinical diagnosis based on history and examination
Plain radiographs including skyline/axial views if instability, arthritis, or bony pathology is suspected
MRI reserved for atypical, refractory, or locking symptoms to assess cartilage and other structures
Assessment of hip and lower-limb biomechanics and muscle strength
Consider hip imaging in adolescents to exclude referred hip pathology
redFlags: True locking, giving way, or significant effusion suggesting internal derangement
Fever, systemic symptoms, or a hot swollen joint suggesting infection or inflammatory arthritis
Night pain, rest pain, or a mass raising concern for tumour
Adolescent knee pain that may be referred from serious hip pathology
reference.prognosis: Many improve with structured rehabilitation, but symptoms can be persistent or recurrent in a substantial minority, particularly if strength and biomechanical deficits are not corrected; long-term association with patellofemoral osteoarthritis is debated.
pitfalls: Labelling all anterior knee pain as chondromalacia and relying on rest alone
Neglecting hip and gluteal strengthening and focusing only on the knee
Missing patellar instability, referred hip pathology, or tumour
Rushing return to sport without addressing training load and biomechanics
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Make structured physiotherapy the mainstay, combining quadriceps strengthening with hip abductor and external-rotator strengthening and movement retraining
Modify aggravating loads such as stairs, squatting, and prolonged sitting with graded activity and relative rest
Use patellar taping or bracing and, in those with excessive foot pronation, foot orthoses as adjuncts to reduce pain
Offer only short-term simple analgesia, recognising its limited role
Address footwear, training errors, and lower-limb biomechanics identified on single-leg squat testing
Educate patients on self-management and reassure them, reserving specialist referral for refractory or atypical cases as surgery is rarely indicated
